scope: 20 existing short, original and explicitly first-school-mock-eligible AQA Year 1 Pure Mathematics cards: proofs, vectors, graph transformations, rational function restrictions, inequalities, tangent normals, trigonometry, signed integration and total positive area.
purpose: Retain each original card and progress ID; check 20 new accepted paraphrases and 40 specific wrong concepts through production answer marker, including 29 existing accepted alternatives.
safeguards: Exact ID, original subject/stage, active true, mock eligibility, unchanged original front/back guards.
The first school mock remains Year 1 Pure only: excluded inverse/composite Year 2 functions and Statistics/Mechanics remain out of scope.
Retain existing correct variants; do not overwrite originals or modify saved progress or cloud sync.
Neither application proofs nor drawn vectors are replaced by these short-recall marking tests.
No multi-mark exam questions disguised as flashcards.

rows.subject: Maths
rows.originalFront: What is proof by exhaustion?
rows.originalBack: Check every possible case in a finite set of possibilities.
accept: Demonstrate the statement in every case in a finite, exhaustive list.
reject: Proving one numerical example establishes a claim for every integer.
Assume the opposite is true and derive a contradiction instead of checking each case.

rows.subject: Maths
rows.originalFront: What does proof by deduction involve?
rows.originalBack: Logical steps from stated assumptions to a justified conclusion.
accept: Use a sequence of justified logical deductions from assumptions to the claimed result.
reject: Check only two numerical examples and assume the conclusion is universally true.
State the conclusion without connecting it logically to the assumptions.

rows.subject: Maths
rows.originalFront: After using tan⁻¹(y/x) for a vector's angle, what should you check?
rows.originalBack: The quadrant, using the signs of both components.
accept: Use the signs of both coordinates to choose the correct quadrant for the direction angle.
reject: Use tan inverse y over x without checking which quadrant the vector lies in.
Use the vector magnitude alone to determine the direction angle.

rows.subject: Maths
rows.originalFront: For a > 0, what is the horizontal scale factor of y = f(ax)?
accept: The horizontal scale factor is one over a, so every x-coordinate is divided by a.
reject: It is a horizontal stretch by a, so each x-coordinate is multiplied by a.
It is a vertical stretch that multiplies y-coordinates by a.

rows.subject: Maths
rows.originalFront: For a>1, what does y = af(x) do to y = f(x)?
rows.originalBack: A vertical stretch by scale factor a.
accept: A vertical stretch by scale factor a: multiply each y-coordinate by a.
reject: The x-coordinates are multiplied by a, producing a horizontal stretch.
The graph is translated a units upwards rather than stretched.

rows.subject: Maths
rows.originalFront: What does y = f(−x) do to the graph?
accept: Mirror the graph in the vertical y-axis by replacing x with negative x.
reject: Reflect the graph in the horizontal x-axis, changing the sign of the outputs.
Translate the graph left without reflecting it.

rows.subject: Maths
rows.originalFront: What does y=|f(x)| do to a graph?
rows.originalBack: Reflects any part below the x-axis in the x-axis; parts above stay unchanged.
accept: Reflect only negative output portions above the x-axis and leave positive portions unchanged.
reject: Reflect in the y-axis instead of the x-axis.
Reflect positive and negative portions across the x-axis, rather than keeping positive ones unchanged.

rows.subject: Maths
rows.originalFront: What happens to an inequality sign when multiplying by a negative number?
accept: Multiplying or dividing both sides by a negative reverses the inequality direction.
reject: Multiplying by a negative leaves the inequality sign unchanged.
Multiplying by any positive number always reverses the inequality.

rows.subject: Maths
rows.originalFront: For an upward-opening quadratic with two distinct roots, where is f(x)>0?
accept: For an upward parabola it is positive to the left of the smaller root and to the right of the larger root.
reject: For an upward parabola the function is positive only between its two real roots.
The only positive function values occur exactly at the two roots.

rows.subject: Maths
rows.originalFront: What are the asymptotes of y = k/x when k≠0?
accept: The coordinate axes are asymptotes: x equals zero and y equals zero.
reject: Both asymptotes are x equals k and y equals k.
It has a vertical asymptote at zero but no horizontal asymptote.

rows.subject: Maths
rows.originalFront: When cancelling a common factor from an algebraic fraction, what restriction must be retained?
rows.originalBack: Any input that made the original denominator zero remains excluded.
accept: Keep excluding inputs that zero the original denominator, even when a factor cancels.
reject: After cancelling a factor, any original zero denominator value becomes permitted.
Exclude every zero of the original numerator even if the denominator is nonzero.

rows.subject: Maths
rows.originalFront: What does a definite integral of f(x) below the x-axis contribute?
rows.originalBack: Negative signed area, not automatically positive physical area.
accept: The region below the horizontal axis contributes a negative value to the definite integral.
reject: Every area below the x axis automatically contributes a positive integral value.
Regions below the axis always contribute zero to the integral.

rows.subject: Maths
rows.originalFront: For total area where a graph crosses the x-axis, what is needed?
rows.originalBack: Split at the roots and add the positive areas.
accept: Split at all roots in the interval, integrate each piece, then add the positive area magnitudes.
reject: A single signed integral always gives total positive area even when regions cancel.
Subtract the size of every region lying below the x-axis to find total positive area.

rows.subject: Maths
rows.originalFront: Magnitude of vector (a,b)?
accept: Take the square root of the sum of squares of its two components.
reject: The magnitude equals a squared plus b squared without taking a square root.
The magnitude always equals the absolute value of a plus b.

rows.subject: Maths
rows.originalFront: How do position vectors give the vector from A to B?
accept: Subtract the position vector of A from the position vector of B to get AB.
reject: Subtract OB from OA to calculate AB.
Add OA and OB together to obtain the vector AB.

rows.subject: Maths
rows.originalFront: What is k times the vector (a,b)?
accept: Multiply the first and second components of the vector by k.
reject: Multiply only the first component by k and leave the second unchanged.
Add k to both components rather than multiplying them.

rows.subject: Maths
rows.originalFront: What is a counterexample?
rows.originalBack: One example showing a universal claim is false.
accept: One concrete case for which a supposed universal mathematical statement is false.
reject: One matching example that agrees with the claim proves it is universal.
To provide a counterexample, check every case in the finite domain.

rows.subject: Maths
rows.originalFront: If the tangent gradient is m≠0, what is the normal gradient?
accept: Use minus one divided by m, the negative reciprocal of the tangent gradient.
reject: The normal has the same gradient m as the tangent.
The normal has gradient one divided by m, with no negative sign.

rows.subject: Maths
rows.originalFront: At which angles in degrees is tan θ undefined?
accept: Tan is undefined at ninety degrees plus any integer multiple of one hundred and eighty degrees.
reject: Tan is undefined at every multiple of one hundred and eighty degrees.
Tan is undefined at zero degrees and one hundred and eighty degrees.

rows.subject: Maths
rows.originalFront: How do you add 2D vectors (a,b) and (c,d)?
accept: Add matching coordinates componentwise to give a plus c and b plus d.
reject: Multiply the components pairwise to obtain ac and bd.
Subtract components to obtain a minus c and b minus d.
